description:
Hi, I'm Ishant Arora from India. I came up with the idea for EarthAudia, researched it, and built it. I love learning how technology works and turning complex ideas into simple, meaningful experiences. Our team built a tool that lets everyone experience Earth science through sound. Aryan Nandan researched my idea and helped shape it into a project. The Earth is speaking. Are you listening? Visit my website to hear it for yourself. This is original work. 

https://earthaudia.earth
summary: EarthAudia is an interactive Earth jukebox that turns NASA Earth science into sound, in real time. NASA collects an enormous amount of Earth data, and most of it arrives as charts, maps and images. Those visuals leave out everyone who cannot see them, and they rarely make anyone feel the change. EarthAudia opens that data to the ear. You can upload any Earth image and hear it played live by a radar beam, type any place on Earth and hear its own 30 second piece of music, blend two places into one piece, and play 146 years of warming from 1880 to 2025 and hear the pitch climb as the planet warms. It answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by building the one thing NASA does not have yet, a live, interactive tool that lets anyone experience Earth science through sound, with no recording and no login. It matters because sound reaches people that charts never reach, including blind and low vision listeners, children, and anyone in a museum or classroom who wants to feel what the data means.
details: EarthAudia is a web tool that turns NASA Earth data into music you can hear and play with, live in your browser. Open earthaudia.earth and you see a real 3D globe with live satellites and live natural events. Pick a dataset and the tool plays it. Upload any Earth image, for example a NASA Earth Information Center frame, and a radar beam scans it live, turning pixel brightness and colour into notes. A built in star cluster photo works the same way. Type any latitude and longitude, or tap the map, and Loc Sound writes a 30 second piece for that place, in any of 19 instruments and 10 melody styles. Blend mixes two places into one 30 second piece. A line on the map joins the two places and shows the distance in km, like a mark in a game, so you can see how far apart the two sounds are. The flow melody walks smoothly from note to note, inspired by Google Magenta, and a soft root note plays underneath. Play the GISTEMP soundtrack and 146 years pass in order, from 1880 to 2025, the pitch rising as the planet warms. Compare two years side by side, hear your birth year, or play the 60 second Earth Heartbeat. Live feeds bring in Delhi weather, NASA EONET natural events, NASA DONKI space weather, and the live orbit of the ISS and Suomi NPP from CelesTrak TLE data. Blind Mode speaks the numbers and hides the visuals, Classroom Mode enlarges the controls for a lesson, and voice commands let you play, pause and switch modes hands free. You can download any sound as a WAV file. The benefit is simple. Sound makes Earth data felt, not just seen, so it reaches blind and low vision people, children, and museum and classroom visitors who would never read a chart. I hope EarthAudia becomes a public exhibit that lets anyone hear the planet change, and hear a place they love. I built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Web Audio API for live sound, Three.js for the 3D globe, Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map, and a small serverless proxy that fetches NASA data so no API key is stored in the browser.
